title: The Central Limit Theorem for Sample Means (Averages)

slides.title: A sampling distribution
slides.body: A sampling distribution describes a statistic across repeated samples of the same size.
slides.question: What would one point represent in a distribution of sample means?

slides.title: Data or sample means?
slides.body: Imagine 1,000 independent random samples of 25 package masses, with one mean calculated per sample.
slides.question: Would a histogram of those means display 25,000 masses or 1,000 means?

slides.title: Sample size versus repetitions
slides.body: Sample size n is the number of observations in each average. A simulation draws 1,000 samples of 25 observations each.
slides.question: Which number is n in the standard-error formula?

slides.title: An observation and an average
slides.body: X represents one observation; X̄ represents the mean of n observations.
slides.question: Which variable describes the average mass of 25 packages?

slides.title: Center of the sample means
slides.body: For independent observations from one population, the mean of the sample mean equals the population mean.
slides.question: If the population mean is 500 g, where is the sampling distribution centered?

slides.title: Standard error
slides.body: The standard error of a statistic is the standard deviation of its sampling distribution.
slides.question: Does standard error describe variability among individual masses or among sample means?

slides.title: Standard error of the mean
slides.body: For n independent observations with common population SD σ, the standard error is σ divided by the square root of n.
slides.question: For σ=20 g and n=25, what is the standard error?

slides.title: SD versus standard error
slides.body: Model: package masses have SD 20 g. Independent samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: Which spread belongs to one mass, and which belongs to the sample mean?

slides.title: Changing sample size
slides.body: Model: population SD is 20 g. Compare independent samples of n=25 and n=100.
slides.question: How does the standard error change?

slides.title: Reducing standard error
slides.body: Model: independent sampling gives standard error 4 g at n=25.
slides.question: What sample size would reduce standard error to 2 g?

slides.title: The central limit theorem
slides.body: The central limit theorem for means says averages of independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance become approximately normally distributed as n grows.
slides.question: Does this theorem say that the individual observations become normal?

slides.title: An exactly normal population
slides.body: The mean of independent normal observations is normal for every positive sample size.
slides.question: If masses are normal, do we need n≥30 to give their sample mean a normal distribution?

slides.title: A skewed population
slides.body: Model: individual download durations are strongly right skewed, with finite mean and variance.
slides.question: Would a sample mean from n=8 automatically have an approximately normal distribution?

slides.title: No universal cutoff
slides.body: The sample size needed for a useful normal approximation depends on the population shape and the desired accuracy.
slides.question: Why might n=30 be insufficient with strong skewness or extreme outliers?

slides.title: Independence
slides.body: The formula σ/√n assumes independent observations.
slides.question: Could 50 measurements taken moments apart from one unstable machine behave like 50 independent observations?

slides.title: Sampling without replacement
slides.body: When sampling without replacement, a sample no larger than 10% of the population is a common independence approximation.
slides.question: Would n=200 from a population of 500 comfortably meet that guideline?

slides.title: A sampling model
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20), measured in grams. Samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: What normal model describes the sample mean?

slides.title: Standardizing an average
slides.body: A sample mean is standardized using its standard error.
slides.question: For μ=500, σ=20, and n=25, what z-score belongs to X̄=508?

slides.title: An upper-tail average
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20). Samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: What is P(X̄>508)?

slides.title: A lower-tail average
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20). Samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: What is P(X̄<496)?

slides.title: An average within a range
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20). Samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: What is P(496<X̄<504)?

slides.title: A percentile of sample means
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20). Samples contain 25 packages.
slides.question: What is the 95th percentile of the sample-mean distribution?

slides.title: Quartiles of sample means
slides.body: Synthetic independent durations have μ = 12 s and σ = 4 s. Samples have n = 64; use a normal approximation.
slides.question: What are Q1, Q3, and the IQR of the sample means?

slides.title: A specified standard-error distance
slides.body: Model: population mean 50 seconds, SD 12 seconds. Independent samples contain 36 observations.
slides.question: What sample mean is 1.5 standard errors above the population mean?

slides.title: One value versus a mean
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20).
slides.question: Which is more likely: one mass above 508 g or a mean of 25 masses above 508 g?

slides.title: The population remains variable
slides.body: Model: population SD is 20 g. Increase the sample size from 25 to 100.
slides.question: Does the spread of individual masses shrink?

slides.title: A surprising sample mean
slides.body: Model: independent masses follow N(500,20). A synthetic sample of 100 has mean 507 g.
slides.question: How unusual is that mean under the model?

slides.title: From probability to inference
slides.body: A population mean is unknown. A random sample mean is observed.
slides.question: How could the sampling variability of means help estimate the unknown population mean?

title: The Central Limit Theorem for Sums

slides.title: A sample sum
slides.body: A sample sum totals the observations in a sample.
slides.question: For shipment weight, would we need an individual mass, sample mean, or sample sum?

slides.title: Mean and sum
slides.body: A sample sum equals the sample size times its mean.
slides.question: If 40 packages have mean mass 500 g, what is their total mass?

slides.title: The center of sums
slides.body: For n observations from a population with mean μ, the expected sum is nμ.
slides.question: If one item has mean mass 50 g, what is the expected mass of 100 items?

slides.title: The spread of sums
slides.body: For n independent observations with common SD σ, the sum has SD σ√n.
slides.question: If σ=4 g and n=100, what is the SD of total mass?

slides.title: Recovering sample size
slides.body: Synthetic independent observations have σ = 6. Their sum has standard deviation 42.
slides.question: What sample size produced this sum?

slides.title: Independent variation
slides.body: Model: individual item masses have SD 4 g; 100 items are independent.
slides.question: Why would using 100×4 g as the SD of total mass overstate its spread?

slides.title: Increasing the total sample
slides.body: Model: independent items have mean mass 50 g and SD 4 g.
slides.question: How do the mean and SD of the sum change when n rises from 100 to 400?

slides.title: A sum can be normal
slides.body: A sum of independent normal observations is normal for every sample size.
slides.question: What model describes the total of 100 independent N(50,4) masses?

slides.title: A normal approximation for sums
slides.body: The central limit theorem for sums makes totals of many independent, identically distributed observations approximately normally distributed when variance is finite.
slides.question: What information about strong skewness would you want before using that approximation?

slides.title: Standardizing a total
slides.body: The z-score of a sum uses the sum's mean and standard deviation.
slides.question: For μ=50, σ=4, and n=100, what z-score belongs to a total of 5,080 g?

slides.title: A total above a limit
slides.body: Model: 100 independent item masses follow N(50,4), in grams.
slides.question: What is the probability that their total exceeds 5,080 g?

slides.title: A total below a limit
slides.body: Model: 100 independent item masses follow N(50,4), in grams.
slides.question: What is the probability that their total is below 4,960 g?

slides.title: A total within a range
slides.body: Model: 100 independent item masses follow N(50,4), in grams.
slides.question: What is the probability that their total lies between 4,940 and 5,060 g?

slides.title: A capacity cutoff
slides.body: A percentile of sums is a cutoff for total values. Model: 100 independent masses follow N(50,4), in grams.
slides.question: What capacity would exceed the total mass in 99% of shipments?

slides.title: A specified distance for a sum
slides.body: Model: independent observations have mean 50 g and SD 4 g. Each sample contains 100 observations.
slides.question: What total lies 1.5 standard deviations above the mean of the sums?

slides.title: An equivalent event
slides.body: A shipment contains exactly 100 items.
slides.question: What event involving the sample mean is equivalent to a total above 5,080 g?

slides.title: The same standardized distance
slides.body: Model: 100 independent masses follow N(50,4). A total is 5,080 g.
slides.question: Do the sum and its corresponding mean have different z-scores?

slides.title: Sums versus averages
slides.body: Model: individual masses have SD 4 g. Compare independent samples of 25 and 100.
slides.question: Does increasing n make sums or averages less variable in their original units?

slides.title: A skewed population total
slides.body: Model: independent task durations are exponential with mean and SD 6 minutes. A batch has 100 tasks.
slides.question: What approximate normal model describes total duration?

slides.title: Checking dependence
slides.body: A shared machine adjustment can shift every item's mass in the same shipment.
slides.question: Would the independent-sum SD formula still be justified?

slides.title: Defining the correct total
slides.body: Model: item masses average 50 g. Each shipment adds a fixed 200 g container.
slides.question: What is the expected total mass of a container holding 100 items?

slides.title: Choosing the random variable
slides.body: A manager asks whether a batch of 80 independent jobs averages more than 7 minutes per job.
slides.question: Should the probability model describe one duration, a mean, or a sum?

slides.title: One observation
slides.body: Model: independent task durations follow an exponential distribution with mean 6 minutes.
slides.question: What is the probability that one task takes longer than 8 minutes?

slides.title: An average of observations
slides.body: Model: independent task durations are exponential with mean and SD 6 minutes. A batch contains 100 tasks.
slides.question: What is the approximate probability that its mean exceeds 7 minutes?

slides.title: Comparing the two events
slides.body: Model: independent task durations are exponential with mean 6 minutes.
slides.question: Would one task longer than 7 minutes be as unusual as 100 tasks averaging longer than 7 minutes?

slides.title: A total duration
slides.body: Model: independent task durations are exponential with mean and SD 6 minutes. A batch contains 100 tasks.
slides.question: What is the approximate probability that its total exceeds 700 minutes?

slides.title: An equivalent threshold
slides.body: A batch contains exactly 100 tasks.
slides.question: Why do a mean exceeding 7 minutes and a total exceeding 700 minutes describe the same event?

slides.title: A mean percentile
slides.body: Model: independent exponential task durations have mean and SD 6 minutes. Samples contain 100 tasks.
slides.question: What is the approximate 90th percentile of sample mean duration?

slides.title: A sum percentile
slides.body: Model: independent exponential task durations have mean and SD 6 minutes. Samples contain 100 tasks.
slides.question: What is the approximate 90th percentile of total duration?

slides.title: A uniform population
slides.body: Model: independent processing times follow U(2,10), in seconds.
slides.question: What population mean and SD are needed to analyze a sample mean?

slides.title: A uniform mean
slides.body: Model: independent processing times follow U(2,10). Samples contain 64 jobs.
slides.question: What approximate model describes their mean time?

slides.title: A lower-tail mean
slides.body: Model: independent processing times follow U(2,10). Samples contain 64 jobs.
slides.question: What is the approximate probability that their mean is below 5.5 seconds?

slides.title: A uniform total
slides.body: Model: 64 independent processing times follow the uniform distribution U(2,10), in seconds.
slides.question: What is the approximate probability that their total is below 350 seconds?

slides.title: A uniform mean percentile
slides.body: Model: 64 independent times follow U(2,10), in seconds.
slides.question: What is the approximate 90th percentile of their sample mean?

slides.title: A uniform total percentile
slides.body: Model: 64 independent times follow U(2,10), in seconds.
slides.question: What is the approximate 90th percentile of their total?

slides.title: Quartiles and IQR of sample means
slides.body: Model: independent observations have mean 20 min and SD 4 min. Samples contain 100 observations. Use a normal approximation.
slides.question: What are the sample-mean quartiles and IQR?

slides.title: Quartiles and IQR of sums
slides.body: Model: independent observations have mean 20 min and SD 4 min. Samples contain 100 observations. Use a normal approximation.
slides.question: What are the sum quartiles and IQR?

slides.title: A central interval for totals
slides.body: Synthetic independent durations are exponential with mean 8 min. Sum 64 durations; use the normal approximation.
slides.question: Between which two totals does the middle 80% lie?

slides.title: Checking the approximation
slides.body: Model: independent processing times follow U(2,10). A normal approximation is used for a mean of 64 times.
slides.question: Can the true sample mean ever be below 2 seconds?

slides.title: A population shape problem
slides.body: Synthetic data show strong right skew and several extreme outliers. A random sample contains 12 observations.
slides.question: Is a normal approximation for its mean automatically justified?

slides.title: A selection problem
slides.body: A large sample includes only files that finished downloading successfully.
slides.question: Can a small standard error remove bias caused by excluding failed downloads?

slides.title: The law of large numbers
slides.body: Under suitable conditions, the average of independent observations approaches the population mean as sample size grows.
slides.question: Does this guarantee that every larger sample mean is closer to μ than the previous one?

slides.title: Two different ideas
slides.body: The law of large numbers concerns closeness to μ; the central limit theorem concerns the distribution of standardized averages.
slides.question: Which idea supports approximating sample-mean tail probabilities with a normal curve?

slides.title: A repeated-sample experiment
slides.body: Use synthetic independent draws from U(0,12), in minutes. For each n, collect many sample means.
slides.question: What changes would you expect in histograms for n=1, n=5, and n=50?

slides.title: Normal approximation to the binomial
slides.body: A binomial distribution counts successes in n independent constant-p trials. For sufficiently large expected counts, a normal distribution can approximate it.
slides.question: What mean and standard deviation should approximate B(100, 0.4)?

slides.title: Approximation conditions
slides.body: OpenStax requires np > 5 and nq > 5, with q = 1 − p; both at least 10 generally improve the approximation.
slides.question: Would B(100, 0.02) meet these conditions?

slides.title: The approximating normal model
slides.body: For X ~ B(n,p), use a continuous Y with the same mean and standard deviation.
slides.question: For X ~ B(100, 0.4), what are the parameters of Y?

slides.title: Continuity correction factor
slides.body: The continuity correction factor 0.5 matches each discrete integer k to a continuous interval from k − 0.5 to k + 0.5.
slides.question: Why should a normal approximation to P(X = 40) use an interval rather than one point?

slides.title: At least: continuity correction
slides.body: Model: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Approximate using Y ~ N(40, √24).
slides.question: Which boundary and normal tail approximate P(X ≥ 45), and what probability results?

slides.title: At most: continuity correction
slides.body: Model: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Approximate using Y ~ N(40, √24).
slides.question: Which boundary and normal tail approximate P(X ≤ 45), and what probability results?

slides.title: More than: continuity correction
slides.body: Model: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Approximate using Y ~ N(40, √24).
slides.question: Which boundary and normal tail approximate P(X > 45), and what probability results?

slides.title: Fewer than: continuity correction
slides.body: Model: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Approximate using Y ~ N(40, √24).
slides.question: Which boundary and normal tail approximate P(X < 45), and what probability results?

slides.title: Exactly: continuity correction
slides.body: Model: X ~ B(100, 0.4). Approximate using Y ~ N(40, √24).
slides.question: Which two boundaries approximate P(X = 45), and what probability results?

slides.title: Checking the approximation
slides.body: For X ~ B(100, 0.4), use software to find the exact P(X ≥ 45).
slides.question: How does it compare with the continuity-corrected normal approximation?

slides.title: Predicting precision
slides.body: Model: independent observations have population SD 12.
slides.question: What sample size gives a standard error of 1?

slides.title: An observed mean
slides.body: Model: independent normal durations have mean 20 and SD 8 minutes. A synthetic sample of 64 has mean 22.
slides.question: How many standard errors above the modeled mean is this result?

slides.title: Unknown population mean
slides.body: A synthetic random sample has n=64, mean 22 minutes, and sample SD 8 minutes.
slides.question: Which population quantity would a confidence interval try to estimate?

slides.title: A claim about the mean
slides.body: A process is claimed to average 20 minutes. A random sample averages 22 minutes.
slides.question: Why should sample size and variability matter before judging that claim?
